all_domain_answers.justification: RDQ is a standardized 24-item disability checklist with a 0–24 score and higher scores indicating greater disability. The report states that the Iranian version was valid and reliable and reports Cronbach's alpha of 0.82 in this sample. The method is appropriate for the disability outcome.

The report states that the same questionnaire battery was administered at baseline, end of treatment, and 12-month follow-up; SMC also completed the same battery at follow-up. All groups' RDQ values are reported at post-treatment and follow-up, with the same RDQ instrument and scoring. The methods do not identify a group-specific assessment method or threshold.
unknowns: The report does not give detailed assessor administration procedures by group.

all_domain_answers.justification: RDQ is a patient-completed checklist, so the patient is the assessor. The report says participants were blinded to random assignment, but the spouse-assisted, patient-only, and usual-care interventions were visibly different; participants probably knew which treatment they received.
unknowns: The report does not explain how participant blinding was maintained despite the visibly different interventions.

counterevidence.implication: The report's statement that participants were blinded to random assignment weighs against awareness, though the intervention formats make awareness of treatment probable.

2.4.1 Primary outcome variables

disability caused by pain. Items reflect the daily activi-

number of items checked by the patient, with higher
scores representing greater disability. The score there-
fore can range from 0 to 24. The RDQ has shown good
psychometric properties in different studies of CLBP
patients (Roland and Morris, 1983; Stratford et al.,
1994, 1998; Roland and Fairbank, 2000). The Iranian
version of RDQ has also shown to be valid and highly

invention, compared to that of SA-CST alone, ET
alone, and standard medical care (SMC). In addition to
better patients' self-efficacy and pain coping outcomes,
the addition of ET to SA-CST enhanced patients'
physical fitness more than did SA-CST alone. The
authors concluded that SA-CST plus ET can improve
physical fitness, pain coping and self-efficacy.
To date, studies of SA-CST have targeted patients
with minimally disabling arthritis pain. Thus, it is not
known whether SA-CST can help CLBPs that suffer
high levels of psychological distress and physical dis-
ability. Furthermore, none of the studies have exam-
ined whether SA-CST can enhance the outcomes of a
short-term comprehensive multidisciplinary treatment
programme, which is typically needed to treat more
disabling pain.
Hence, the objective of this study was to investigate
the efficacy of a SA-CST protocol for patients under-
going a multidisciplinary pain management pro-
gramme (SA-MPMP), providing patients and spouses
with educational information about CLBP along with
systematic training in cognitive and behavioural pain
coping skills. Both partners attended the sessions of
individual instructions and couple pain coping skills.
These additional couple-focused coping skills were
designed to supplement and reinforce other learned
pain coping skills. Additionally, based on the patients'
general or specific needs, individual/group sessions
with an orthopaedic surgeon, physiotherapist and/or
psychiatrist were provided.
The efficacy of SA-MPMP was investigated in
comparison with two other treatments. The first com-
parator was a conventional patient-oriented multi-
disciplinary pain management programme (P-MPMP).
This intervention focused on patients only, and used
similar training materials and services as delivered to
patients in the SA-MPMP arm. The second comparator,
SMC consisted of medically based treatment that pro-
vided patients with pain medication.
It was hypothesized that, in comparison to P-MPMP
and SMC, SA-MPMP would lead to better psychosocial
outcomes for patients with CLBP.
2. Methods
2.1 Setting and participants
Participants were consecutive patients with CLBP
referred to two pain clinics located in Iran University of
Medical Sciences (IUMS). Participants were recruited
over the course of 5 months. Eligible participants were
screened based on inclusion/exclusion criteria. To be
included, patients had to be between the ages of 18 and
70 years, married and referred to the pain clinic with
low back pain of greater than 6 months duration.
Exclusion criteria were (1) pain that could be explained
by an identified pathological process (e.g., arthritis,
cancer) or vertebral fracture, spinal inflammatory
disease or infection, malignancy, current nerve root
pathology, spondylolysis, lumbar spondylosis, spondy-
lolisthesis; (2) pregnancy; (3) insufficient command of
the Persian language; (4) active rheumatological
disease,
progressive
neurological
disease,
serious
cardiac or other internal medical condition, malignant
basic diseases, acute traumas, infections, or acute vas-
cular catastrophes; (5) major cognitive dysfunction; (6)
coexisting psychiatric morbidity as determined by a
psychological screening interview [checking for major
psychiatric disorders according to Diagnostic and Sta-
tistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM IV) criteria];
and (7) history of participation in another rehabilita-
tion programme that employed cognitive behavioural
principles.
A total of 36 patients enrolled in the study and were
randomly assigned to one of the three conditions.
Three participants dropped out of the SA-MPMP con-
dition (two dropped out before treatment, one discon-
tinued treatment after the fourth session), and one
participant dropped out from SMC group. There were
no dropouts in the P-MPMP group. (Fig. 1) The study
was approved by the ethical research committee of
IUMS.
2.1.1 Demographics and pretreatment
assessments
The total sample consisted of 29 women and 4 men,
aged ranged 24 to 67 years [mean 45; standard devia-
tion (SD) 10]. Pain duration ranged 6 to 276 months
(median 74), with no significant between-group dif-
ferences. In addition to CLBP, one patient also
reported a recent acute neck pain.
2.3 Randomization procedure
A
simple
randomization
technique
was
applied.
Patients were randomized to the three groups in
blocks of 12 using a software-generated randomiza-
tion plan. They were coded consecutively; the first 12
were assigned to P-MPMP, the second 12 to SA-MPMP
and the last 12 to SMC. Participants were blinded to
their random assignment, but investigators and treat-
ment staff were not blinded to the randomization.

Work capability increased over time in both groups. In

A. Functional Restoration Program. This program, very
similar to that described in detail by Mayer et al,21 focused
particularly on self-responsibility, activity, and a multidisci-
plinary approach.
Schedule. One characteristic of a full-time FR program is
that its schedule is comparable with a usual work situation
regarding the number of work hours, thus giving the partici-
pant the feeling of being able to manage a job (Table 2). Ac-
cording to work habits in the United States, FR programs there
usually are 9 hours a day, whereas FR programs in Europe
usually last 8 hours daily. Most FR programs involve 3 weeks
of treatment because this long enough to improve the partici-
pant's function significantly, and yet not so long that the par-
ticipant gets the feeling that permanent treatment is needed.

The same BPI 0–10 NRS measure was used on the same scheduled occasions for all groups, including before each session and at Week 25. No group-specific measurement threshold or detection opportunity is reported.

Primary outcome
The primary outcome measure was the mean change from base-
line over the course of 25 (Group Time interaction) in average
pain intensity from the BPI20 (scored on a 0-10 NRS with 0 = no
pain and 10 = maximal pain). Baseline average pain intensity was
assessed at inclusion then on the day of randomization, just before
the first rTMS session (Day 1) and corresponded to the average of
these two values. Pain intensity was further assessed immediately
before each rTMS session at Days 2, 3, 4, 5 then at Weeks 2, 3, 4, 6,
8, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, then 3 weeks after the last rTMS session at
Week 25.

eh_5cb78524e470c011.quote:
Procedures
Inclusion took place 2 to 4 weeks before randomization. Patients
were assessed for inclusion and exclusion criteria, including the
BPI and DN4 questionnaire (Douleur Neuropathique en 4 ques-
tions). Other assessments were performed at randomization and
immediately before the first rTMS session, then before subsequent
rTMS sessions for up to 3 weeks after the last rTMS session (at
Week 25). Assessments were limited to assessment of pain inten-
sity, percentage of pain relief and Patient and Clinician Global
Impression of Change (PGIC, CGIC) from Days 2 to 5 after the first
session, then at Weeks 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 13, 16, 19 and 22 or extended
to additional measures (pain quality, sensory and affective dimen-
sions of pain, sleep, anxiety, depression, catastrophizing and qual-
ity of life) at Weeks 2, 4, 10, 19 and 25.

answer.justification: Although clinical judgments could be susceptible, the report states that the investigators considered bias in assessment of the composite components unlikely; it also used an assignment-blinded expert committee for the six BPD classifications requiring judgment in place of an indicated oxygen-reduction test. The component definitions use established clinical criteria, and no evidence shows that knowledge changed any assessment. Thus influence was possible but is not likely on the available evidence.
unknowns: Blinding and actual influence for routine NEC and BPD assessments are not reported in detail.

all_domain_answers.justification: The composite combines death, NEC defined by Bell stage IIa or higher, and moderate-to-severe BPD defined using oxygen or ventilatory support at 36 weeks after at least 28 days of oxygen, with established criteria and an oxygen-reduction test when indicated. These are appropriate clinical outcomes and established operational criteria; there is no indication that the method was invalid or insensitive to plausible intervention effects.

Both randomized groups were assessed for the same prespecified composite at 36 weeks using the same component definitions. The report describes outcome data for all participants and does not identify different ascertainment schedules or detection opportunities by group. This supports probably no, although the report does not detail every component's assessment process separately by arm.
unknowns: Arm-specific operational details for ascertainment of NEC and BPD are not separately reported.

all_domain_answers.justification: The trial was unblinded and most clinical component assessments were therefore likely made by staff who knew treatment assignment. The report identifies blinding only for the committee that classified BPD in the six cases without an indicated oxygen-reduction test; it does not report blinded assessment for other NEC or BPD cases.
unknowns: The identities and masking status of assessors for all individual NEC and BPD determinations are not specified.

all_domain_answers.justification: Knowledge could influence clinical determination of NEC at the Bell stage IIa threshold and BPD severity when applying oxygen-reduction or support criteria. Death, another component, is objective and not meaningfully influenced by assessor awareness; however, awareness could affect the clinically judged components of the composite.

Although clinical judgments could be susceptible, the report states that the investigators considered bias in assessment of the composite components unlikely; it also used an assignment-blinded expert committee for the six BPD classifications requiring judgment in place of an indicated oxygen-reduction test. The component definitions use established clinical criteria, and no evidence shows that knowledge changed any assessment. Thus influence was possible but is not likely on the available evidence.
unknowns: Blinding and actual influence for routine NEC and BPD assessments are not reported in detail.

answer_anchors.text: Knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.
Knowledge could have influenced assessment but it was not likely to do so.

question.bias_construct: Whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced outcome assessment. Require evidence or strong beliefs plus a judgement opportunity; awareness alone does not establish influence.
considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
Objective components can provide valid reassurance for those components without overriding likely influence or unresolved Evidence for subjective components in the same Result.
question.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms or recovery assessed by an intervention provider. A standardized scale or grading rule does not by itself remove an elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment pathway.
evidence_needed: Evidence of actual influence or strong beliefs and judgement opportunities that make influence likely, given the assessor and outcome.
question.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of influence cannot be judged; this question is conditional on possible influence in 4.4.
question.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which knowledge of intervention status could have influenced outcome assessment but there is no reason to believe that it did from those in which knowledge of intervention status was likely to influence outcome assessment. When there are strong levels of belief in either beneficial or harmful effects of the intervention, it is more likely that the outcome was influenced.
question.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.5
question.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 4.4: Is it likely that assessment of the outcome was influenced by knowledge of intervention received?

Outcomes
The primary outcome was a composite of necro-
tizing enterocolitis (defined as Bell's stage IIa or
higher),15 moderate-to-severe bronchopulmonary
dysplasia, or death as assessed at a postmen-
strual age of 36 weeks. In accordance with the
international standard criteria of Bancalari and
Claure,16 bronchopulmonary dysplasia was defined
as the need for supplemental oxygen or positive-
pressure ventilatory support at a postmenstrual
age of 36 weeks after at least 28 cumulative days
of supplemental oxygen. This diagnosis includ-
ed the performance of an oxygen reduction test
according to the criteria of Walsh et al.,17 if indi-
cated (see the Supplementary Methods). If the
indicated oxygen reduction test was not per-
formed, a committee of three investigators who
had extensive clinical expertise and who were
unaware of trial-group assignments assessed the
severity of bronchopulmonary dysplasia as mild
or moderate. All outcome measures and their
definitions are summarized in Table S2.

Primary Outcome
At 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, data regarding
the composite primary outcome were available
for all 273 infants. In 6 infants, the indicated
oxygen reduction test had not been performed,
so the severity of bronchopulmonary dysplasia
was classified by the committee. A primary-
outcome event occurred in 63 of 136 infants
(46.3%) in the expectant-management group and
in 87 of 137 infants (63.5%) in the early-ibupro-
fen group (absolute risk difference, -17.2 per-
centage points; upper boundary of the one-sided
95% confidence interval [CI], -7.4; P<0.001)
(Table 2).
